name: Zane Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is a normal day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and fit door frames, partitions and timber edges on building sites. I have a vocational trade certificate and an ordinary carpenter's wage, not a foreman's job. On the school extension I like leaving a neat edge; hauling warped timber up wet stairs wears me out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like, and do you use AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner and I have two school-age children and a mortgage. We have about four months of expenses saved, and there are some other contractors nearby if I need one. I use an AI chatbot now and then to make a shopping list or read a specification, but I trust the tape measure more than its answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the site crew the software can tidy a delivery note, but it won't hang a fire door straight. We have enough awkward corners to keep carpenters busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My pay is ordinary for the trade, and we have four months of bills saved. The mortgage and two schoolchildren make me watch our spending, but the current building contract and a few other local contractors leave me steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll finish the school extension's door frames and keep checking the opening with a tape before cutting. Each payday we'll set aside a small new amount for the mortgage, as long as the hours stay normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. The mortgage is there every month, but a bit quicker paperwork would give me a longer stretch with the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did the paperwork miss a detail on site?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week a door schedule said a frame was square, but the plaster edge bowed by a finger's width. I cut the timber to the wall I could see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does setting money aside mean in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I mean about fifty from each weekly pay packet, not taking money out of the four-month reserve and naming it savings again. My partner and I would check the total after three months.

say: **Door fitting** still needs a tape and someone who can read an uneven wall.
**Quicker paperwork** would be useful without changing our site jobs much.
think: Four months of **saved bills** and a current contract make this manageable.
The **mortgage** still needs attention with two children at school.
do: **Finish** the school extension door frames and check openings before cutting.
**Set aside** fifty from each weekly pay packet while hours remain normal.
feel: **Calm** about steady site work, though the mortgage remains on my mind.
S0.quote: I cut the timber to the wall I could see.
fieldNote: He uses **site measurements** to settle a mismatch between drawings and an uneven wall.
The modest **new saving** comes from future weekly pay, conditional on normal hours, while the current reserve stays intact.

steps.text: Finish school extension door frames and check openings with tape
Set aside fifty from weekly pay while site hours stay normal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say office drawings and buying lists may get quicker, then site robots may handle repetitive carries later. I'd want the foreman to ask the carpenters before changing how a wall is built.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A computer making the cutting list could save time, but a wrong list can leave us waiting unpaid between contracts. I have some local contractors I could call, yet I'd rather keep this crew's hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll mark the next three delivery lists against what we actually use on the school site and give the differences to our foreman. If an AI list is introduced, I'll try it on a small room after another carpenter has checked it, then keep a record of wasted trips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because the office may send us neat numbers that don't match a crooked room. I don't expect my own carpentry hours to vanish soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the materials list is wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a bad list back before the delivery truck leaves, then ask for the missing board in writing. A wrong board can hold up six doors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide an AI list has earned your trust?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paper cutting list and the measured room beside the AI version. If it works on three small rooms, I would use it for the next one rather than fight it on principle.

say: **Office lists** can speed up, but carpenters must check real room sizes.
**Site robots** may come later than changes to drawings and buying.
think: A wrong **cutting list** can cost a site day between contracts.
My own **carpentry hours** still look fairly secure, with some other local contractors.
do: **Mark** three delivery lists against materials used on the school extension.
**Trial** an AI cutting list on one small room after a carpenter checks it.
feel: **Anxious** about bad office instructions; I still expect regular site work.
S1.quote: A wrong board can hold up six doors.
fieldNote: He trusts new lists after a **measured trial**, which fits his steady rather than early adopter approach.
His feared cost is **wasted site time**; he does not yet predict a loss of his own carpentry hours.

steps.text: Mark three school site delivery lists against materials used
Trial AI cutting list on small room after carpenter checks it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AI by 2028 might redraw the school extension and order its doors, but robots around 2031 are the point when fitting work itself could change. I'd ask which tasks the builder actually plans to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be about 48 when capable site robots arrive. If a contractor needs half as many carpenters, our income is exposed. Four months of savings won't carry our mortgage through a long cut in carpentry wages, and other local builders may buy the same site robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll ask the foreman for the next year's carpentry orders and whether paid training for setting out robot work exists. My partner and I will price the mortgage against one income; if a paid site technician course is offered with a real place, I'd enrol and attend the first sessions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing site days, though there is time to ask and train. I'd still be working age with children at school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner to look at the mortgage statement with me before we change any family plans. The children's school routine is one thing I want to protect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the site technician course worth taking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need wages during the course and a certificate that local building firms recognise. If the offer is only an unpaid brochure, I'd keep looking for paid carpentry work instead.

say: **2028 thinking AI** reaches drawings and orders before robots can fit doors around 2031.
The builder should say which **site tasks** it actually plans to change.
think: At about **48**, I could lose paid carpentry days when robots reach sites.
Four months of **savings** cannot cover a mortgage through a long gap.
do: **Ask** foreman about next year's carpentry orders and paid training places.
**Compare** mortgage payments with one household income this month.
**Enrol** in recognised site technician course if a paid place is offered.
feel: **Anxious** about hours, with time to seek paid training.
S2.quote: Four months of savings won't carry our mortgage through a long cut in carpentry wages, and other local builders may buy the same site robots.
fieldNote: His **training decision** requires a paid place and a certificate local builders recognise; a brochure changes nothing.
A site robot could shrink **paid carpentry days** by about 2031, while the mortgage and school routine limit his room to gamble.

steps.text: Ask foreman about carpentry orders and paid site technician training
Compare mortgage payments against one household income
Enrol in recognised site technician course if paid place offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say 2031 thinking AI could do the drawings while trades still build, and capable site robots around 2034 give us a longer warning. Five years is enough to test work on an actual building, not just watch a machine at a show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be about 51 when robots do hands-on site work. If our builder cuts carpentry hours, I still need the mortgage wage, but five years gives me a chance to add a trade before that happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask our foreman whether the company will pay for evening building-services training and release me for the assessment days. If the funding and time are agreed, I'll enrol next term; meanwhile I'll keep taking carpentry jobs and add to our reserve from normal pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible cut, but I can use five years better than two. I would rather earn a building-services ticket than guess which site robot wins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why building-services training rather than another carpentry ticket?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd choose building services because a site still needs someone to trace a leak or check a door seal behind a finished wall. My trade certificate gives me a base, but it isn't that qualification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What exactly must the employer agree to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd need written release for assessment days and the course fee paid before I sign up. If those are missing, I would keep the carpentry rota and ask local firms about vacancies.

say: **2031 thinking AI** may redraw plans before hands-on robots reach sites around 2034.
A real **site trial** and funded training are more useful than a trade-show demonstration.
think: At about **51**, I would still need wages if robots reduce carpentry hours.
Five years could let me earn **another qualification** if the builder covers its cost.
do: **Ask** foreman for course fees and paid assessment release in writing.
**Enrol** in building-services training next term if both are agreed.
**Add** to the mortgage reserve from normal pay while hours last.
feel: **Anxious** about possible hour cuts, with a workable training window.
S3.quote: I would rather earn a building-services ticket than guess which site robot wins.
fieldNote: He proposes a **different trade qualification**, conditional on employer funding and paid release, rather than treating an enquiry as retraining.
The five-year runway supports **new saving from pay** while he remains employed; the existing four-month reserve is separate.

steps.text: Ask foreman for building-services course fees and paid assessment release
Enrol in building-services course if fees and paid release agreed
Add to mortgage reserve from normal pay while hours last

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI in 2036 changes the paperwork, then capable robots around 2039 reach the building site. By then the school extension will be long finished, so we should be planning for new sites, not that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be about 56 when robots can do the carpentry, with the children older and the mortgage hopefully smaller. A decade makes the income risk easier to manage, but I cannot promise the loan will be gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the trade certificate current and ask at our annual site review what building-services work the contractor expects to keep. My partner and I will review the mortgage balance each year and put new pay into it whenever we have room after the children’s costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious rather than frightened. Ten years is a long time in building work, but I want the household numbers on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which household numbers would you check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the actual loan balance, the interest rate and our monthly payment, not just say we are doing fine. That will show whether extra repayments are possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make another contractor a real option?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A smaller firm nearby would need to advertise a paid role with hours that cover our mortgage. I would apply if our contractor later cuts the carpentry rota, not resign now for a rumour.

say: **2036 thinking AI** precedes robots doing carpentry around 2039.
A decade lets workers check **future site demand** and household costs.
think: At about **56**, I may face less carpentry work, but our mortgage might be smaller.
The **loan balance** cannot be assumed away while children still cost money.
do: **Keep** trade certificate current and ask about future site work annually.
**Review** mortgage balance and interest rate with partner each year.
**Pay extra** toward mortgage from new pay when household costs allow.
feel: **Anxious** about long-term demand, with time to manage the loan.
S4.quote: I would check the actual loan balance, the interest rate and our monthly payment, not just say we are doing fine.
fieldNote: He treats the **2039 robot date** as a long household budgeting horizon, not an assumed retirement date.
He would change employers only after a **real rota cut** and for an advertised paid role that covers the mortgage.

steps.text: Keep trade certificate current and ask contractor about future site work
Review mortgage balance and interest rate with partner yearly
Pay extra toward mortgage from new pay when costs allow

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because site robots around 2031 could arrive while our mortgage is still heavy. Clear plans for carpentry hours and a paid, recognised site technician place would help me make a move without dropping the wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to the half-built site when a machine gets the timber count wrong. A school wall cannot wait for a perfect spreadsheet while the carpenters lose a day's pay. I want the plan checked against the actual rooms.

headlineQuote: A school wall cannot wait for a perfect spreadsheet while the carpenters lose a day's pay.
portrait: **Zane**, 43, is an experienced site carpenter with a vocational trade certificate and ordinary trade pay.
His partner and two schoolchildren share a **mortgage** with him, while four months of expenses sit in reserve.
He uses AI **now and then**, trusts measured site trials, and has some other local contractors to call.
Faster robots make him **anxious** about paid carpentry days; a longer runway supports conditional training and new mortgage payments.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** may bring capable site robots around 2031 while the mortgage still needs his trade wage.
whatWouldHelp: Clear **carpentry-hour plans** and a paid, recognised site technician place would help him change without losing wages.
